artists.biography: Salad were a UK-based alternative rock group formed in London in 1992, that included Dutch vocalist/keyboardist Marijne van der Vlugt, bassist Pete Brown, drummer Rob Wakeman (ex-Colenso Parade), and guitarist Paul Kennedy. In 1996, Charley Stone (later of Gay Dad) joined the band as a live guitarist, keyboard player and backing vocalist.

Salad.biography: Salad were a UK-based alternative rock group formed in London in 1992, that included Dutch vocalist/keyboardist Marijne van der Vlugt, bassist Pete Brown, drummer Rob Wakeman (ex-Colenso Parade), and guitarist Paul Kennedy. In 1996, Charley Stone (later of Gay Dad) joined the band as a live guitarist, keyboard player and backing vocalist.

perplexity.description:
Salad - Drink Me (1995)

Salad's debut album Drink Me, released in May 1995 on Island Records, exemplifies the European indie-pop sensibility that distinguished certain Britpop-era acts from their more guitar-driven British counterparts. Fronted by Dutch former MTV Europe veejay Marijne van der Vlugt, the band paired her distinctive crystalline, whispery vocals with shimmery, soaring indie-pop arrangements crafted by her English bandmates. The album's sonic palette—delicate and atmospheric rather than aggressive—set Salad apart within the broader Britpop landscape, which was typically dominated by louder, more masculine-oriented guitar rock.

Drink Me achieved modest commercial success, reaching number 16 on the UK album charts. Notable tracks including "Motorbike To Heaven," "Drink The Elixir," and "Granite Statue" demonstrated the band's visual and sonic sophistication, with each accompanying music video reflecting a distinctly European aesthetic that diverged from both American and mainstream British '90s styles. The album emerged following Salad's initial breakthrough supporting Blur on tour in 1993, positioning them as one of several female-fronted satellite acts within Britpop's broader ecosystem.

Though Drink Me remains arguably Salad's strongest work from the era, the band gradually faded from mainstream consciousness by the decade's end. The album stands as a testament to the diversity within mid-'90s alternative rock, capturing a moment when European indie-pop aesthetics briefly intersected with British guitar-based trends.
